This isn’t really news anymore since everyone knows about it already… However, I do believe that certain types of media shouldn’t be available to minors without parental consent. For example, R-rated movies aren’t allowed unless accompanied by adults over eighteen; likewise, mature video game ratings require proof of identity before purchase. These restrictions exist primarily because many studies show negative effects associated with exposure during childhood development stages – especially aggression among boys between five and ten years old after watching violent television programs regularly throughout adolescence.[1][2]. In addition:
* There’s evidence suggesting excessive consumption leads towards desensitization toward real-life situations involving physical harm;
* Exposure increases risk-taking behavior later down life path including substance abuse problems related alcoholism / drug addiction ;
* And finally , long term memory impairment caused directly correlated amount hours spent viewing screen entertainment versus non-screen activities .
So while banning outright might seem extreme solution given current state affairs ; implementing stricter guidelines around access points could potentially help mitigate potential harms posed future generations .

[ANS] Three-Dimensional Structure of Protein That Controls Cell Division Revealed by Scientists at RIKEN and Nagoya University (Press Release)
The three dimensional structures for a family of proteins called septins have been revealed in unprecedented detail. The research, led jointly from Japan’s National Institute of Genetics (NIG) and Kyoto Sangyo University with collaborators including scientists from the RIKEN SPring-8 Center , has implications not only for understanding how cells divide but also potentially for treating diseases such as cancer.
Septin is an important component of cellular membranes where it plays key roles during processes like cytokinesis—the final stage when two daughter cells separate after dividing—and vesicle trafficking—where molecules are transported between different parts of the membrane via small sacs known as transporters or ‘vesicles’. Septum can be found throughout eukaryotic organisms—from yeast to humans—but its exact function remains unclear because until now no one had managed to determine what shape they take up inside living cells.
To solve this problem researchers used cryo-electron microscopy—a technique which allows them to freeze samples so quickly that water does not crystallize around their surface before being imaged—to visualize individual septums within intact human red blood cells . They then combined these images into 3D models using computer software developed specifically for analyzing large datasets generated through electron microscopes .
“The results show us exactly why we need both techniques,” says lead author Dr Masahiro Ueda who works on structural biology at NIG “We were able to see things about septum organization never seen before.”
One surprise was finding out just how flexible each molecule could become under certain conditions; something previously thought impossible given previous studies suggesting rigid shapes instead! This flexibility may help explain some aspects related disease progression especially since mutations affecting specific regions might cause changes leading towards abnormal growth patterns etcetera…
Another interesting discovery came regarding interactions amongst neighboring subunits – there appears strong evidence supporting idea whereby adjacent units form stable complexes capable holding onto cargo while moving along cytoskeleton network thus facilitating efficient delivery process!
Overall findings provide valuable insight into workings behind fundamental biological mechanisms governing life itself…

A team led by researchers at MIT has developed an entirely different approach for making qubits that could be more practical than existing methods — while also being easier to scale up into large numbers needed for useful applications such as error correction.
The work is described this week in Nature Physics , in a paper co-authored by graduate student Yifan Hou; professors William Oliver (head of the Quantum Engineering Group), Dirk Englund, Vladimir Bulović, Marin Soljačić, and John Joannopoulos; postdoc Shuo Sun; former visiting scientist Xingyao Wu ’18 PhD; alumnus Jie Wang SM ‘17; undergraduate students Zhi-Xun Shen '20 and Michael Zhang '21; and others.
Qubit stands for “quantum bit,” which refers not only to its function but how it works: Qubits are based around two fundamental properties of atoms called spin states . generated_texts.raw_completion:
's nose can detect cancer
[NEWS] 2018-11-13 (Tue) 10:00 ~ 12:30, 14:20~16:50 / 1F Conference Room A
The dog’s sense of smell is much more sensitive than that of humans. In fact it has been used to sniff out drugs and explosives at airports.
Now scientists are training dogs in the UK to identify lung cancers by their scent alone – a process known as “electronic noses”.
They hope this could lead to an early diagnosis for patients who have no symptoms but whose tumours may be detected on scans or blood tests.
In one study published last year , researchers trained two Labrador retrievers called Daisy and Keela using samples from people with non-small cell lung carcinoma - which accounts for about eight out nine cases worldwide .
Daisy was able to correctly distinguish between healthy volunteers’ breaths and those containing volatile organic compounds produced when cells divide rapidly during disease progression . She also identified some individuals without any signs of illness before they were diagnosed through routine screening programmes .
Keela had similar success rates identifying both malignant tumors among asymptomatic subjects undergoing surveillance imaging studies after treatment completion ; however she did not perform well enough overall compared against other detection methods currently available commercially such as CT scanning technology so further research needs done here too!
This new approach offers promise because there aren’t many options right now if someone doesn't show typical warning signals like coughing up phlegm etc.. It might help catch things earlier though we need larger trials first!
